title: One-dimensional Quantum Gibbs States In Constant Circuit Depth
authors: Sa\'ul Pilatowsky-Cameo, Georgios Styliaris, Ainesh Bakshi, Daniel Malz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the Gibbs state of any spin chain can be exactly decomposed into a mixture of product states over contiguous blocks of qubits with bounded length, at any constant temperature. As a consequence, any such Gibbs state can be prepared by local unitary circuits of constant depth, with efficient classical preprocessing. We place strong limits on the spatial structure of thermal entanglement: both the entanglement depth and entanglement width (measures of multiparticle entanglement) are bounded by constants, while the localizable entanglement (the bipartite entanglement that can be generated with the aid of local measurements and classical communication) vanishes exactly beyond a constant threshold distance. Our result also has implications for quantum thermalization: for any translation-invariant spin-chain Hamiltonian with nondegenerate spectral gaps, typical low-complexity pure states drawn from a maximally entropic ensemble at any constant effective temperature become locally indistinguishable from the Gibbs state upon unitary evolution. Additionally, we obtain an analogous decomposition for fermionic systems: the Gibbs state of any 1D local fermionic Hamiltonian is exactly a mixture of constant-depth local fermionic circuits acting on Gaussian states.
tldr: The paper proves that any 1D quantum Gibbs state can be decomposed into a mixture of product states over bounded-length blocks, allowing constant-depth circuit preparation and bounding entanglement measures.
motivation: Understanding the entanglement structure and preparation complexity of thermal states is key to quantum simulation and thermalization, but exact decompositions were previously unknown.
method: They analytically show that Gibbs states of any spin chain can be expressed as a convex combination of product states on contiguous blocks of constant length, and extend the result to fermionic systems using Gaussian states and fermionic circuits.
result: Consequently, entanglement depth and width are bounded by constants, localizable entanglement vanishes beyond a constant distance, and typical low-complexity states thermalize in the sense of local indistinguishability from the Gibbs state.
conclusion: This establishes strong limits on thermal entanglement and shows that Gibbs states can be efficiently prepared, with implications for quantum thermalization and fermionic systems.

title: Characterizing Quantum Precision Enhancement For Multiple Currents In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Khalak Mahadeviya, Sheikh Parvez Mandal, Mahasweta Pandit, Javier Prior, Mark T. Mitchison, Saulo V. Moreira
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The kinetic uncertainty relation (KUR) constrains fluctuations of individual currents in classical nonequilibrium systems in terms of the dynamical activity, which quantifies the average number of transitions per unit of time. Here, we derive a multi-current KUR (MKUR) establishing the precision limit for multiple currents generated in classical stochastic processes in the nonequilibrium steady state. We then apply our theory to identify quantum devices whose correlated current fluctuations surpass this classical limit by comparing the quantum system to a classical emulator with the same average currents in the steady state. In this way, violations of the emulator's MKUR have a clear physical meaning, i.e., that the quantum-coherent evolution reduces joint current fluctuations below what is possible for a classical Markovian system with the same energy-level structure and incoherent resources. Since the MKUR incorporates correlations between currents, its violation pinpoints nonclassical fluctuations in parameter regimes where the single-current KUR is satisfied. We illustrate the essential and complementary role of these bounds for characterizing joint current precision with two examples: a coherently driven two-level system and an experimentally motivated model of a three-level heat engine subject to parasitic environmental couplings.
tldr: The paper derives a multi-current kinetic uncertainty relation (MKUR) to set precision limits on correlated currents in nonequilibrium steady states and uses it to identify quantum coherent enhancements in open quantum systems.
motivation: Classical kinetic uncertainty relations constrain individual current fluctuations, but it is unclear how quantum coherence affects the precision of multiple correlated currents and where nonclassical advantages arise.
method: They derive a multi-current KUR for classical stochastic processes and compare quantum systems to a classical emulator with the same average steady-state currents, so that violations of the emulator's MKUR signal genuinely quantum-coherent reductions in joint current fluctuations.
result: They show that quantum coherence can violate the MKUR, reducing joint current fluctuations below the classical Markovian bound even in regimes where the single-current KUR is satisfied, and illustrate this with a coherently driven two-level system and a three-level heat engine with parasitic couplings.
conclusion: The MKUR provides a physically meaningful tool for characterizing nonclassical precision enhancement in open quantum systems and for distinguishing quantum from classical current fluctuations in thermodynamic devices.

The authors then propose using the MKUR as a classical benchmark: by constructing a classical emulator that reproduces the average currents of a quantum system, any violation of the emulator's MKUR signals that quantum coherence reduces joint current fluctuations below classical limits. This provides a clear physical interpretation of nonclassical fluctuations, even when the single-current KUR is satisfied. The theory is illustrated with two examples: a coherently driven two-level system and a three-level heat engine with parasitic environmental couplings. In both cases, the MKUR reveals nonclassical precision in parameter regimes where single-current bounds are not violated, demonstrating the essential role of correlations. The work thus offers a systematic tool to identify quantum devices that outperform classical stochastic machines in terms of joint current precision.

title: Conversable Quantum Fire In The Standard Model
authors: Ofer Casper, Barak Nehoran, Or Sattath
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum fire consists of quantum states that can be efficiently functionally cloned but cannot be transmitted using one-way classical communication. Whereas all previous quantum-fire constructions with proven untelegraphability are relative to an oracle, ours, based on one-shot signatures, is in the standard model. Our construction achieves two further notions that we introduce: (a) keyless untelegraphability, a strengthening of untelegraphability; and (b) conversability, meaning that a flame, though not telegraphable via one-way classical communication, can be transmitted via classical interaction. Hence one-way and two-way classical communication differ qualitatively in their power to transmit this quantum fire. We use these two novel properties of quantum fire, along with its clonability, to give one of the first cryptographic applications of quantum fire. Keyless untelegraphability forces the distribution of serial numbers of valid flames to have high min-entropy, while conversability and clonability allow the corresponding flame to be cloned and transferred using only classical communication. We present two variants of our conversable quantum-fire construction. The first, based on one-shot signatures (instantiable from subexponential iO, subexponentially secure one-way functions, and LWE), supports polynomially many flames, and super-logarithmic min-entropy of the serial-number distribution. The second, under the stronger assumption of exponentially unforgeable one-shot signatures (instantiable relative to a classical oracle), supports exponentially many flames, and linear min-entropy.
tldr: The paper constructs conversable quantum fire in the standard model from one-shot signatures, achieving keyless untelegraphability and showing that one-way and two-way classical communication differ qualitatively for transmitting such states.
motivation: Previous quantum-fire constructions with proven untelegraphability were only relative to an oracle, and the power of one-way versus two-way classical communication for transmitting quantum states was not well understood.
method: The authors build quantum-fire states from one-shot signatures, instantiable from subexponential indistinguishability obfuscation, subexponentially secure one-way functions, and LWE, or from exponentially unforgeable one-shot signatures relative to a classical oracle.
result: They obtain two variants: one supporting polynomially many flames with super-logarithmic min-entropy of serial numbers, and another supporting exponentially many flames with linear min-entropy under stronger assumptions.
conclusion: The construction gives one of the first cryptographic applications of quantum fire, using keyless untelegraphability to force high min-entropy serial numbers and conversability plus clonability to enable classical-only transfer.

title: Separability Rigidity Of Gaussian States Under Positive Domination
authors: Peter van Loock Evgeny Shchukin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a separability rigidity theorem for finite-mode Gaussian states. Let [MATH] be Gaussian and let [MATH] be a fixed partition of the modes. If [MATH] dominates a nonzero positive operator [MATH] that is separable across [MATH], [MATH], then [MATH] itself is separable across [MATH]. The dominated operator is arbitrary and need not be Gaussian. As consequences, convex mixing among finitely many separability partitions creates no new Gaussian states: a Gaussian state belonging to such a convex class is already separable across one fixed partition. In particular, full inseparability and genuine multipartite entanglement coincide for finite-mode Gaussian states, and identical copies of a biseparable Gaussian state cannot activate genuine multipartite entanglement. We also show that the implication cannot be reversed by constructing a fully separable Gaussian state that dominates a positive multiple of a genuine multipartite entangled state.
tldr: A separability rigidity theorem shows that a finite-mode Gaussian state dominating a nonzero separable positive operator must itself be separable across the same partition, with strong consequences for multipartite Gaussian entanglement.
motivation: The work addresses whether separable operators can constrain or witness entanglement in Gaussian states, and whether convex mixing or copies can create or activate genuine multipartite entanglement beyond full inseparability.
method: The authors prove a rigidity theorem for finite-mode Gaussian states under positive domination by arbitrary separable operators, and derive consequences for convex mixing and entanglement activation.
result: For finite-mode Gaussian states, domination by a separable operator implies separability; full inseparability and genuine multipartite entanglement coincide, and identical copies of a biseparable Gaussian state cannot activate genuine multipartite entanglement. The converse fails via a fully separable Gaussian state dominating a positive multiple of a genuine multipartite entangled state.
conclusion: This establishes strong separability rigidity for Gaussian states, clarifies the multipartite entanglement structure, and constrains entanglement activation in Gaussian settings.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper proves a separability rigidity theorem for finite-mode Gaussian states: if a Gaussian state ρ_G dominates a nonzero positive operator T that is separable across a fixed mode partition I (i.e., 0 ≠ T ≼ ρ_G), then ρ_G itself must be separable across I. Crucially, T is arbitrary and need not be Gaussian. This result is then applied to show that convex mixing among finitely many separability partitions cannot create new Gaussian states: any Gaussian state in the convex hull of states separable across various partitions is already separable across one fixed partition. As a corollary, for finite-mode Gaussian states, full inseparability coincides with genuine multipartite entanglement, and identical copies of a biseparable Gaussian state cannot activate genuine multipartite entanglement. The authors also demonstrate that the implication is not reversible by constructing a fully separable Gaussian state that dominates a positive multiple of a genuine multipartite entangled state, showing that domination of a separable operator is sufficient but not necessary for separability of the Gaussian state.
key_contributions: Proves a separability rigidity theorem: if a Gaussian state dominates any nonzero separable operator across a partition, then the Gaussian state is separable across that partition.
Shows that convex mixing among finitely many separability partitions cannot produce new Gaussian states: any Gaussian state in such a convex class is already separable across one fixed partition.

Constructs a fully separable Gaussian state that dominates a positive multiple of a genuine multipartite entangled state, proving the implication is not reversible.

The key technical step is to show that if a Gaussian state ρ_G dominates a separable operator T, then the covariance matrix and mean of ρ_G must satisfy conditions compatible with separability across the given partition. This may involve analyzing the support of T and using properties of positive operators under Gaussian channels or partial transposition. The argument is non-constructive and does not require T to be Gaussian, which broadens the applicability. The consequences for convex mixing and entanglement activation follow from the rigidity theorem by considering convex combinations of Gaussian states separable across different partitions and applying the theorem to the mixture. The non-reversibility is shown by explicit construction, likely using a separable Gaussian state with a covariance matrix that allows domination of an entangled state's positive multiple, exploiting the fact that domination does not imply separability of the dominator.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is a strong rigidity property: for Gaussian states, the existence of any dominated separable operator forces the state itself to be separable. This is surprising because domination is a weak condition—T can be arbitrarily small and non-Gaussian. The corollaries have significant implications for entanglement theory: they show that convex mixing of Gaussian states across different partitions cannot create genuine multipartite entanglement, and that full inseparability is equivalent to genuine multipartite entanglement in the Gaussian setting. The non-reversibility result highlights a fundamental asymmetry: a separable Gaussian state can dominate an entangled state, so domination is not a necessary condition for separability. title: Collectivity Limits Quantum Entanglement
authors: Tomotaka Kuwahara Donghoon Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding what limits many-body quantum entanglement is a central problem in physics. Spatial locality has long provided a fundamental mechanism: correlations between a region and its complement must be mediated through a small spatial interface, thereby constraining their entanglement. Here we show that universal constraints on entanglement can persist even when interactions are strongly nonlocal, through collectivity: many weak interactions suppress collective quantum fluctuations while retaining a finite overall interaction scale. We establish this mechanism rigorously for generic gapped Hamiltonians with Kac-normalized power-law interactions [MATH] on a [MATH]-dimensional lattice. For arbitrary bipartitions, we prove that the ground-state entanglement scales at most logarithmically with system size for [MATH] and subextensively for [MATH], and remains parametrically stronger than the arbitrary-bipartition bound for [MATH]. Together, these results reveal collectivity as a fundamental mechanism for constraining many-body entanglement alongside spatial locality.
tldr: The paper proves that collectivity from many weak nonlocal interactions can universally constrain ground-state entanglement in gapped many-body systems, even without spatial locality.
motivation: Understanding what limits many-body quantum entanglement is a central problem, and spatial locality has long been the standard mechanism; the authors ask whether entanglement constraints can persist for strongly nonlocal interactions.
method: They rigorously analyze generic gapped Hamiltonians with Kac-normalized power-law interactions on a d-dimensional lattice and derive entanglement bounds for arbitrary bipartitions.
result: For arbitrary bipartitions, the ground-state entanglement scales at most logarithmically with system size in one regime, subextensively in another, and remains parametrically stronger than the arbitrary-bipartition bound in a third regime.
conclusion: Collectivity is identified as a fundamental mechanism constraining many-body entanglement alongside spatial locality.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the fundamental question of what limits many-body quantum entanglement when interactions are not spatially local. The authors introduce 'collectivity' as a new mechanism: many weak, long-range interactions can suppress collective quantum fluctuations while maintaining a finite overall interaction scale, thereby constraining entanglement even in the absence of locality. They rigorously analyze generic gapped Hamiltonians with Kac-normalized power-law interactions r^{-α} on a D-dimensional lattice. For arbitrary bipartitions, they prove that ground-state entanglement scales at most logarithmically with system size for α < D/2 and subextensively for D/2 < α < D. title: Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlators Beyond Lindblad
authors: Elisa Vallini, Felix Fritzsch, Pieter W. Claeys
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) provide a powerful probe of quantum chaos and scrambling. While the Lindblad formalism is often used to describe OTOCs in open systems, microscopic mechanisms that give rise to the Lindblad equation at the level of time-ordered correlation functions do not necessarily justify this approach at the level of OTOCs. Starting from a microscopic model of a subsystem coupled to a random bath, we show that the resulting OTOC dynamics contains an additional contribution compared to the standard Lindblad approach. This contribution, induced by correlations between different replicas, allows key properties of the underlying unitary dynamics such as long-time freeness to be retained and information scrambling to be captured more faithfully. As an application, we show that this extended formalism can be used to numerically study OTOCs in large closed systems by replacing part of the system with a dissipative boundary, offering a way to study operator spreading and higher-order correlations beyond directly accessible system sizes.

result: The extended formalism captures long-time freeness and information scrambling more faithfully, and it is applied numerically to study OTOCs in large closed systems by replacing part of the system with a dissipative boundary.

title: Entanglement Spectrum And Magic In Higher-dimensional Free Fermionic Systems
authors: Beatrice Magni, Daniele Iannotti, Riccardo Travaglino
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study fermionic non-local magic in higher-dimensional free-fermion systems through the lens of the entanglement spectrum. For translationally invariant Gaussian states in strip geometries, dimensional reduction maps the problem to independent lower-dimensional momentum sectors, leading in two dimensions to a multiplicative logarithmic violation of the boundary law analogous to Gioev-Klich-Widom scaling. We further show that the second R\'enyi fermionic non-local magic is bounded by the capacity of entanglement and introduce an entanglement-temperature deformation that probes the low-energy structure of the entanglement Hamiltonian. Applied to the matter-Majorana sector of the Kitaev model, this response is exponentially suppressed in the Abelian phase and algebraic in the non-Abelian phase, where its ratio with the capacity approaches a universal constant. Out of equilibrium, we extend the quasi-particle description to fermionic non-local magic in higher-dimensional quenches and show that random Gaussian circuits exhibit diffusive spreading in two spatial dimensions.

motivation: Understanding non-local magic in free fermionic systems and its relation to entanglement is important for characterizing quantum resources in higher dimensions and out of equilibrium.
method: Dimensional reduction for translationally invariant Gaussian states in strip geometries is used to analyze the entanglement spectrum; a Rényi fermionic non-local magic bounded by the capacity of entanglement is introduced along with an entanglement-temperature deformation.
result: A multiplicative logarithmic violation of the boundary law is found in 2D; the response is exponentially suppressed in the Abelian phase of the Kitaev model but algebraic in the non-Abelian phase, and random Gaussian circuits exhibit diffusive spreading in 2D.
conclusion: The entanglement spectrum provides a powerful lens to study magic in free fermion systems, with distinct signatures in topological phases and non-equilibrium dynamics.

title: Is Rapid Mixing Stable?
authors: Jordi A. Monta\~n\`a-L\'opez, Barbara Roos, Sebastian Stengele, \'angela Capel, Rahul Trivedi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several physically interesting Lindbladians, such as those describing generic open quantum system models as well as engineered state preparation processes, are often rapidly mixing, that is, they relax to steady states in time scaling polylogarithmically with the system size. Owing to the short mixing times, it is physically expected that local perturbations do not substantially increase the mixing time. In this work we question this expectation and ask whether rapid mixing survives. We provide counterexamples showing that rapid mixing is not stable in general, even when the perturbation does not change the steady state. We also show that arbitrarily weak local Hamiltonian perturbations can destroy rapid mixing. Complementing these results, we develop an array of sufficient conditions which imply stable rapid mixing, including several classes of quasifree fermionic systems, commuting Lindbladians, and local spin systems. We also identify conditions under which modified logarithmic Sobolev inequalities (MLSIs), a stronger form of convergence, lead to stable rapid mixing. As a further implication of our results, we show that rapid mixing does not imply a positive MLSI constant.
tldr: The paper investigates whether rapid mixing of Lindbladians is stable under local perturbations, showing it is not stable in general but identifying sufficient conditions for stable rapid mixing.
motivation: Rapid mixing is common in open quantum systems and is often expected to be robust against local perturbations, but this expectation requires rigorous verification.
method: The authors construct counterexamples where local perturbations destroy rapid mixing, and they develop sufficient conditions for stable rapid mixing involving quasifree fermionic systems, commuting Lindbladians, local spin systems, and modified logarithmic Sobolev inequalities (MLSIs).
result: Rapid mixing is not stable in general; arbitrarily weak local Hamiltonian perturbations can destroy it, and rapid mixing does not imply a positive MLSI constant, though certain classes of Lindbladians remain stable.
conclusion: The work clarifies the fragility of rapid mixing under perturbations and provides conditions under which it is stable, with implications for the dynamics of open quantum systems.

The work thus provides a nuanced picture: while rapid mixing is fragile in general, structured classes of systems exhibit stability, and MLSIs serve as a useful tool for certifying robustness.

title: Dynamical Resource Theory Of Time-reversal Symmetry Breaking
authors: Jisho Miyazaki, Kohdai Kuroiwa, Mio Murao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-reversal symmetry and its violation (T-violation) are fundamental across diverse physics domains, from particle physics to fluctuation theorems and reciprocity. While time-reversal symmetry for isolated systems is simply determined by the Hamiltonian, quantifying the magnitude of T-violation, especially in noisy quantum processes, has been a subject of ongoing debate. Here, we propose an operationally meaningful framework to quantify the intrinsic T-violation of quantum channels. We integrate operationally defined time-reversal transformations into dynamical resource theory to formulate T-violation as a resource. T-violation decomposes into two distinct components: kinematic T-violation originating from antiunitary motion-reversal, and nonunitality driven purely by thermodynamics. This decomposition resolves the longstanding confusion between broken time-reversal symmetry and non-invertibility. Finally, we analyze the resulting resource theory of kinematic T-violation, showing that it is neither quality-like nor quantity-like, and proving the existence of a universal golden unit even within classical channels.
tldr: Proposes a dynamical resource theory framework to quantify intrinsic time-reversal violation (T-violation) of quantum channels.
motivation: Quantifying T-violation in noisy quantum processes remains debated, and there is a need to operationally distinguish broken time-reversal symmetry from non-invertibility.
method: Integrates operationally defined time-reversal transformations into dynamical resource theory, decomposes T-violation into kinematic antiunitary and thermodynamic nonunitality components, and analyzes the resulting resource theory of kinematic T-violation.
result: T-violation decomposes into kinematic and nonunital thermodynamic parts, resolving longstanding confusion; the resource theory of kinematic T-violation is neither quality-like nor quantity-like and admits a universal golden unit even for classical channels.
conclusion: Provides an operational resource-theoretic quantification of T-violation with implications for quantum thermodynamics and channel theory.

title: Near-Optimal Parallel Unitary Process Tomography In Diamond Distance
authors: Sisi Zhou Noam Scully
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unitary process tomography is the act of learning how an unknown unitary gate acts on a quantum system. It is an essential procedure for realizing a functioning quantum computer. As quantum technologies develop, it is important to understand the computational resources needed to conduct unitary process tomography using a variety of types of circuits. In particular, when measuring error in diamond distance, it is known how to achieve optimal query complexity using a sequential circuit architecture, but it had not been known whether a parallel circuit architecture could achieve the same optimal query complexity. In this work, we prove that unitary process tomography with near-optimal query complexity is indeed possible using a parallel circuit by introducing an explicit, novel parallel procedure. This closes the gap between sequential and parallel circuits up to a logarithmic factor, showing that parallel and sequential strategies are nearly equally capable for this task.

result: They show that parallel circuits can achieve near-optimal query complexity for unitary process tomography, matching the sequential optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor.
conclusion: Parallel and sequential circuit architectures are nearly equally capable for unitary process tomography in terms of query complexity.

title: Deciding The Attainability Of The Multiparameter Quantum Fisher Information Is NP-Hard
authors: Lorcan O. Conlon, Laura Shou, V Vijendran, Kishor Bharti, Aritra Das, Simon K. Yung, Jacob M. Taylor, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Jun Suzuki, Syed M. Assad
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum Fisher information (QFI) sets a fundamental bound on the attainable precision when estimating multiple parameters simultaneously. Incompatibility among the individually optimal measurements can, in some cases, imply that the precision limit set by the QFI is not attainable. In certain special cases, including pure states and full-rank states, the exact conditions for when the precision limit set by the QFI can be saturated are known. However, general conditions for the attainability of the QFI with measurements on individual copies of the quantum state have long been sought. Indeed, this was recently stated as one of the five problems in quantum information theory highlighted by [P. Horodecki et al, PRX Quantum 3, 010101 (2022)]. In this work we prove that exact attainability with individual measurements is NP-hard to decide, even for a restricted set of real, constant-rank quantum models. The source problem for our proof is the NP-hard problem of deciding whether a given bipartite density matrix is separable or not. Our result shows that the longstanding difficulty in obtaining general conditions for QFI attainability reflects a fundamental computational obstruction, rather than merely a limitation of existing mathematical techniques: unless P=NP, no efficiently computable necessary-and-sufficient criterion can exist in general.

motivation: The QFI sets the fundamental precision limit for simultaneous multiparameter estimation, but general conditions for its attainability have long been sought, and the problem was highlighted as one of five key open problems in quantum information theory.
method: The authors reduce the NP-hard problem of deciding bipartite separability to the problem of deciding exact QFI attainability using individual measurements, constructing a restricted class of real, constant-rank quantum models.
result: They show that exact attainability with individual measurements is NP-hard, implying that no efficiently computable necessary-and-sufficient criterion can exist unless P=NP.
conclusion: The longstanding difficulty in finding general conditions for QFI attainability reflects a fundamental computational obstruction rather than a limitation of existing mathematical techniques.

title: From Classical To Quantum Channels: Achieving Positive Covert Rates
authors: Hassan Zivarifard, Xiaodong Wang, Alexei Ashikhmin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the conditions under which covert communication at positive rates is feasible over discrete memoryless classical, classical-quantum, and quantum channels. For classical point-to-point channels, we show that if the dimension of the channel input probability simplex exceeds that of the channel output probability simplex, equivalently, if the input alphabet has larger cardinality than the output alphabet, then positive covert rates are achievable for certain classes of Discrete Memoryless Channels (DMCs). We further show that allowing the innocent symbol (i.e., the symbol transmitted in the no-communication mode) to be chosen appropriately can enlarge the class of DMCs for which positive covert rates are achievable. We also study covert communication over classical Multiple-Access Channels (MACs), where the additional transmitter effectively enlarges the set of available channel input pairs, and we show that the conditions required to satisfy the covertness constraint are less restrictive for MACs than for point-to-point channels. We extend these results to classical-quantum DMCs by showing that if the dimension of the input probability simplex exceeds the affine dimension of the set of output states that can be induced at the channel output, then positive covert rates are achievable for certain classes of classical-quantum DMCs. Finally, for quantum channels, we show that if the innocent state (i.e., the state transmitted in the no-communication mode) is mixed, then the covertness constraint can always be satisfied by a non-trivial input ensemble. Consequently, positive covert rates are achievable whenever the legitimate receiver can distinguish at least two states in a suitable such ensemble.

motivation: Covert communication aims to hide the existence of transmission, but positive-rate feasibility over quantum channels is not well understood.
method: Information-theoretic analysis of covertness constraints using probability simplex dimensions, affine dimension of output states, and input ensemble design for DMCs, MACs, and quantum channels.
result: Positive covert rates are achievable when input simplex dimension exceeds output simplex/affine dimension for classical and classical-quantum channels; for quantum channels, a mixed innocent state permits nontrivial input ensembles and positive rates if the receiver can distinguish at least two states.
conclusion: The work extends covert communication theory to quantum settings and identifies channel conditions that enable positive-rate covert transmission.

title: Witness-based Quantification Of non-Markovianity Without Complete Choi State Reconstruction
authors: Pritam Roy, Saheli Mukherjee, Bivas Mallick
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying non-Markovianity is a fundamental problem in the theory of open quantum systems, as it is essential for exploiting environmental memory as a resource in quantum technologies. Existing resource-theoretic and operational quantifiers, however, generally require complete knowledge of the intermediate dynamical map and are therefore experimentally demanding. Here, we develop a witness-based framework for the quantification of non-Markovianity that bypasses complete reconstruction of the Choi state associated with the intermediate dynamical map. We first show that every non-Markovianity witness provides a certifiable lower bound on the geometric resource measure of non-Markovianity and identify the necessary and sufficient conditions under which this bound is tight. Motivated by the fact that non-positive-semidefinite witnesses are generally difficult to measure in real experimental scenario, we then focus on positive-semidefinite witnesses, which admit a natural implementation as positive operator valued measure (POVM) elements. We prove that every positive witness yields a certified lower bound on the Rivas--Huelga--Plenio (RHP) measure, thereby establishing a complete hierarchy connecting witness-based quantification, the RHP measure, and the geometric distance measure. Applying our framework to amplitude-damping and general Pauli dynamics, we find that the optimal positive witnesses reduce to simple Bell-parity projectors. Furthermore, we show that the resulting witness values can be obtained directly from a small number of experimentally accessible correlation measurements, thereby eliminating the need for complete Choi-state reconstruction and providing an efficient and experimentally feasible approach for the quantification of non-Markovianity in open quantum systems.
tldr: The paper develops a witness-based framework to quantify non-Markovianity without reconstructing the full Choi state, using positive-semidefinite witnesses implementable as POVMs.
motivation: Existing non-Markovianity quantifiers typically require complete knowledge of the intermediate dynamical map, which is experimentally demanding, so a more accessible witness-based approach is needed.
method: The authors prove that every non-Markovianity witness gives a certified lower bound on the geometric resource measure, and that positive witnesses yield lower bounds on the RHP measure, forming a hierarchy; they apply this to amplitude-damping and Pauli dynamics.
result: Optimal positive witnesses reduce to simple Bell-parity projectors, and witness values can be obtained from a few experimentally accessible correlation measurements, avoiding full Choi-state reconstruction.
conclusion: This provides an efficient and experimentally feasible route to quantify non-Markovianity in open quantum systems, with implications for using environmental memory as a resource.

title: Bivariate Bicycle Codes Over Group Algebras
authors: Chaobin Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a weighted-shift formulation of bivariate bicycle group-algebra (BBGA) codes over finite group algebras. One binary shift acts by right multiplication and the other by left multiplication; associativity ensures that these shifts commute even for a nonabelian seed group. Bivariate polynomials in the shifts, including mixed monomials, therefore define CSS codes. We give explicit sparsity bounds and distinguish nonabelian seed groups from codes that are intrinsically inequivalent to abelian realizations. For [MATH], a pair of weighted permutation shifts generates a regular [MATH] action and recovers the known [MATH] and [MATH] bivariate bicycle codes. We also present a computer-verified [MATH] code over [MATH], with every check of weight eight. This example belongs to the established nonabelian two-block group-algebra family. Exhaustive low-weight enumeration and an intrinsic stabilizer-support invariant certify that it is inequivalent to any ordinary abelian BB or two-block group-algebra realization, even under qubit permutations combined with local Clifford operations. Finally, a nonuniform weighted-shift construction over [MATH] yields a [MATH] code with check weights six and eight. An exact enumeration of its minimum stabilizer supports rules out every ordinary binary 2BGA realization at that length, under the same equivalence. This establishes that the unrestricted weighted-shift formulation extends beyond the ordinary 2BGA class, even with an abelian seed group.
tldr: The paper introduces a weighted-shift formulation of bivariate bicycle group-algebra codes, yielding new CSS stabilizer codes and proving inequivalence to ordinary abelian realizations.
motivation: Bivariate bicycle codes are promising for quantum error correction, but their group-algebra generalizations and equivalence classes are not fully understood.
method: Uses left and right multiplication shifts that commute via associativity, defines bivariate polynomials in these shifts as CSS codes, derives sparsity bounds, and applies exhaustive low-weight enumeration and a stabilizer-support invariant.
result: Recovers known bivariate bicycle codes and constructs a computer-verified code over a nonabelian group with all checks of weight eight, plus a nonuniform weighted-shift code with check weights six and eight, both inequivalent to any abelian BB or two-block group-algebra realization.
conclusion: The unrestricted weighted-shift formulation extends beyond the ordinary 2BGA class, even with an abelian seed group, expanding the landscape of quantum error-correcting codes.

title: Derivation Of Fokker-Planck Equation And Its Entropy Production
authors: M\'ario J. de Oliveira T\^ania Tom\'e
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive the Fokker-Planck equation and its entropy production from the master equation. To this end we consider a discrete space of states where the master equation is defined and appropriate transition rates are introduced. A transition rate has two parts, one of which is the ordinary term proportional to the inverse of the spacing and the other is inversely proportional to the square of the spacing corresponding to the variance of the independent stochastic variable. In the continuous space limit, we obtain the Fokker-Planck as well as the rate of entropy production and the flux of entropy. We also consider the case where the space of states is the phase space and discuss the equations appropriate for systems in contact with several heat reservoirs and for isolated systems.
tldr: The paper derives the Fokker-Planck equation and its entropy production directly from a master equation by taking the continuous-space limit of discrete transition rates.
motivation: To establish a systematic connection between master-equation dynamics and the Fokker-Planck description, including entropy production and entropy flux, for stochastic systems.
method: A discrete state space with transition rates split into a drift term and a diffusive term is used; the continuous-space limit yields the Fokker-Planck equation, entropy production rate, and entropy flux, with extensions to phase space, multiple heat reservoirs, and isolated systems.
result: The Fokker-Planck equation, entropy production rate, and entropy flux are obtained in the continuum limit, and appropriate equations for systems coupled to several heat reservoirs and for isolated systems are discussed.
conclusion: The work provides a unified derivation linking master equations to Fokker-Planck thermodynamics, offering a framework for analyzing entropy production in classical stochastic and phase-space systems.

The authors introduce transition rates that consist of two parts: a term proportional to the inverse of the lattice spacing (drift) and a term inversely proportional to the square of the spacing (diffusion), the latter corresponding to the variance of an independent stochastic variable. By taking the continuous-space limit, they obtain the Fokker-Planck equation along with expressions for the rate of entropy production and the entropy flux. The derivation is then extended to phase space, where the authors discuss the resulting equations for systems coupled to multiple heat reservoirs and for isolated systems. The work aims to provide a systematic bottom-up approach linking discrete master equations to continuous Fokker-Planck dynamics and thermodynamic quantities.

The rates are split into a deterministic part scaling as 1/Δx and a stochastic part scaling as 1/Δx², which is typical for diffusive processes. By performing a Kramers-Moyal expansion or a systematic Taylor expansion in the limit Δx → 0, they recover the Fokker-Planck equation. The entropy production is derived by analyzing the probability current and its relation to the thermodynamic forces, following standard stochastic thermodynamics techniques. The extension to phase space involves treating position and momentum as continuous variables and incorporating multiple heat reservoirs through appropriate transition rates that satisfy detailed balance with respect to different temperatures.

title: Singleton-Optimal Rank-Metric Css Codes : Equality Structure And Exact Projected-Recovery Radii
authors: Myeongjun Kim, Suseong Lee, Jaeho Jeon, Young-Sik Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Correlated faults from shared control can have dense physical support yet low rank over a base field, motivating rank-metric quantum codes for stacked architectures. We prove an asymmetric rank-metric Singleton bound for Calderbank--Shor--Steane codes, including degenerate codes, and characterize equality through commuting maximum-rank-distance matrix codes. Optimal pairs exist for every admissible parameter triple and are necessarily pure. Comparison with erasure bounds establishes an exact advantage in stacked rank distance for general stabilizer codes at fixed physical resources on certain tall layouts. We determine whether relaxing the recovery target enlarges the worst-case correctable radius. For Singleton-optimal pairs with positive logical dimension, the measured syndrome determines the projected error modulo stabilizers exactly at radii strictly below half the sector rank distance, on every layout and for every nonzero projector. The projected syndrome is recoverable at arbitrary radii exactly when the complementary check space is invariant under the adjoint projector; otherwise, the same radius limit applies. For nontrivial idempotents, this invariance requires more rows than columns or sector distance one. For trace-self-adjoint projectors, linear ambient projected-syndrome interfaces in both sectors exist exactly when the code splits as a tensor product across the projector. Designs placing the two check spaces in complementary projector images are necessarily one-sided whenever they encode logical information. Two explicit families realize the extreme cases of the equality structure, including a two-sided family with an efficient certifying decoder attaining the optimal unique-decoding radius.
tldr: The paper proves an asymmetric rank-metric Singleton bound for CSS quantum codes, characterizes equality, and determines exact projected-recovery radii from syndrome measurements.
motivation: Correlated faults from shared control can have low rank over a base field, motivating rank-metric quantum codes for stacked architectures and requiring fundamental bounds and recovery guarantees.
method: It establishes a Singleton bound for rank-metric CSS codes including degenerate codes, characterizes equality through commuting maximum-rank-distance matrix codes, and analyzes when projected syndromes can be exactly recovered.
result: Optimal pairs exist for every admissible parameter triple and are necessarily pure; the projected syndrome determines the error modulo stabilizers below half the sector rank distance, while arbitrary-radius recovery holds exactly when the complementary check space is projector-invariant.
conclusion: The work provides a structural theory of Singleton-optimal rank-metric CSS codes, identifies explicit extremal families, and gives a certifying decoder attaining the optimal unique-decoding radius.

abstract: ArXiv:2609.36203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of simulating dynamics under geometrically local Lindbladians acting on a lattice of qudits. title: Puncturing For Adaptive Entanglement-Assisted Stabilizer Codes
authors: Nicolai Peder B\"ulow Pedersen, Jakob Kaltoft S{\o}ndergaard, Jaron Skovsted Gundersen, Ren\'e B{\o}dker Christensen, Petar Popovski
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes are essential for reliable quantum communication. The achievable parameters can be improved by using entanglement-assisted stabilizers at the cost of consuming pre-shared Bell pairs. If the availability of such Bell pairs is intermittent, the ability to adapt the code to available resources is beneficial. That is, to pick a single mother code that can be adapted to different entanglement budgets. To achieve this, we extend an existing puncturing construction for standard/unassisted stabilizers to the entanglement-assisted setting through a three-step procedure: Interpreting the code as an unassisted stabilizer, puncturing a receiver-side qubit, and recovering an entanglement-assisted representation. This procedure reduces the number of required Bell pairs by one while preserving the number of transmitted and logical qubits. We derive a bound on the resulting distance loss and establish conditions for preserving the original code distance. Finally, we analyse distinct, randomly generated, entanglement-assisted stabilizers with five to eight transmitted qubits. Of these codes, 14.75% have a greater distance than their associated unassisted representations. Among this subset, 81.4% admit at least one puncturing choice that preserves the original entanglement-assisted distance. These results illustrate how puncturing can reduce entanglement requirements while maintaining code distance.
tldr: The paper extends puncturing to entanglement-assisted stabilizer codes, enabling adaptation to varying Bell-pair budgets while preserving code parameters.
motivation: Entanglement-assisted quantum error correction can improve code parameters but requires pre-shared Bell pairs, which may be intermittently available, motivating adaptive codes from a single mother code.
method: A three-step puncturing procedure interprets the code as unassisted, punctures a receiver-side qubit, and recovers an entanglement-assisted representation; the authors derive a distance-loss bound and test random codes with five to eight transmitted qubits.
result: The procedure reduces required Bell pairs by one while preserving transmitted and logical qubits; among tested codes, 14.75% outperform unassisted counterparts, and 81.4% of those admit distance-preserving puncturing.
conclusion: Puncturing can lower entanglement requirements without sacrificing code distance, providing a useful tool for adaptive entanglement-assisted quantum communication.

title: Out-of-time-order Correlators In Volcano Potentials
authors: Aritra Banerjee, Reetik Jangir, Rishant Sharma
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC) has emerged as an important diagnostic for quantum information scrambling and a key signature of quantum chaos. In this work, we discuss out-of-time-order correlators, analytically and numerically, for the so-called Volcano potentials. This family of potentials parametrically interpolates between bounded wells and confining walls, and includes P\"oschl-Teller as a specific case. Through a combination of numerical diagonalization and semiclassical analysis, we investigate various regimes of the potential parameter regimes containing regions of both positive and negative curvatures. Moreover, we demonstrate in this case that short-time exponential growth of the OTOC does not necessarily signal global quantum chaos; instead, it correlates with the sampling of negative curvature regions by excited states.

method: The authors combine numerical diagonalization with semiclassical analysis to compute OTOCs across parameter regimes of volcano potentials, including the Pöschl-Teller limit.
result: They find that exponential short-time OTOC growth does not necessarily imply global chaos; it correlates with excited-state sampling of negative-curvature regions in the potential.
conclusion: These results refine the diagnostic power of OTOCs and highlight the role of potential geometry in distinguishing local signatures from global chaos.

The rank deficiency of the four-parameter FIM means the reported diagonal ratios are conditional and cannot be interpreted as joint sensitivities, limiting their direct utility for experimental design.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work sits at the intersection of quantum physics and neutrino phenomenology, using quantum information concepts such as entanglement, discord, and quantum Fisher information to analyze open-system dynamics. For a researcher interested in quantum physics broadly, it demonstrates how quantum resource measures and multi-parameter estimation theory can be applied to a concrete physical system—neutrino oscillations—and highlights fundamental limits from measurement incompatibility and rank deficiency. The paper's emphasis on distinguishing dynamical information loss from measurement inaccessibility is relevant to quantum metrology and open quantum systems, while the neutrino-specific benchmarks connect to particle physics and experimental neutrino programs.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper is a technically solid and conceptually clarifying contribution to the quantum-information analysis of neutrino oscillations. Its main novelty lies in the sharp distinction between two dephasing mechanisms and the exact quantum-information characterization of the two-flavor mode state, as well as the explicit demonstration of rank deficiency in the four-parameter FIM for single-energy flavor measurements. The three-flavor benchmark provides useful numerical benchmarks, though the monochromatic approximation and state-level nature limit direct experimental applicability. Overall, it is a valuable methodological study that bridges quantum metrology and neutrino physics, with appropriate caveats about the scope of its conclusions.

title: Chern-number Estimation: Nearly Optimal Quantum Algorithm And Provable Quantum Speedup
authors: Soichiro Imamura, Shintaro Ae, Kazuki Sakamoto, Ryu Hayakawa, Chusei Kiumi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological phases of matter are characterized by global properties of quantum states beyond conventional local order parameters. The Chern number is a central invariant in this characterization, linking the geometry of quantum states to robust physical observables and making its determination key to understanding quantum matter. We construct a nearly optimal quantum algorithm for estimating the Chern number of a smooth Hamiltonian family over a two-dimensional parameter torus with a unique, gapped ground state, including interacting many-body systems. The algorithm transports and reuses two ground-state copies prepared at a single reference point and uses generalized quantum signal processing to coherently accumulate geometric phases. It achieves a Hamiltonian-oracle evolution time of [MATH], where [MATH] bound the parameter derivatives of the Hamiltonian and [MATH] is a known spectral-gap lower bound. We prove a matching worst-case oracle lower bound, even when the Chern number is promised to be zero or one, establishing optimality up to polylogarithmic factors. For local Hamiltonian families with an inverse-polynomial gap and a supplied guiding state, exact Chern-number computation is in [MATH] and is [MATH]-hard, and merely deciding whether the Chern number is zero or one is already [MATH]-complete. These results establish how efficiently quantum computers can estimate a quantized topological invariant and provide evidence for quantum advantage in characterizing topological phases.
tldr: The paper constructs a nearly optimal quantum algorithm for estimating the Chern number of gapped ground states and proves matching lower bounds and complexity hardness results.
motivation: The Chern number is a central topological invariant linking quantum state geometry to robust observables, and its efficient estimation is key to understanding topological phases and demonstrating quantum advantage.
method: The algorithm transports and reuses two ground-state copies from a single reference point and uses generalized quantum signal processing to coherently accumulate geometric phases, with oracle lower bounds and complexity-theoretic reductions.
result: It achieves Hamiltonian-oracle evolution time scaling nearly optimally with parameter derivatives and spectral gap, and shows that exact Chern-number computation is complete for a quantum complexity class even for the zero-or-one promise.
conclusion: These results establish how efficiently quantum computers can estimate a quantized topological invariant and provide evidence for quantum advantage in characterizing topological phases.

title: Quantifying Teleportation Overhead In Distributed Unitary Coupled-Cluster Ans\"atze
authors: Grier M. Jones, Hassan Tariq Shafi, Zixuan Wang, Thomas Trenty, Zachary Vernec, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) has been proposed as a way to scale quantum algorithms for practical applications beyond monolithic quantum processor architectures. Among these applications, quantum chemistry is widely regarded as one of the most promising use cases for quantum computing. In this work, we estimate the distributed-resource requirements of unitary coupled-cluster (UCC) ans\"atze for quantum chemistry, focusing on unitary coupled-cluster singles and doubles (UCCSD), unitary pair coupled-cluster doubles (UpCCD), and unitary pair coupled-cluster with generalized singles and doubles (UpCCGSD) circuits for hydrogen chains. We focus on a teleportation-based approach to DQC, quantitatively comparing a naive distribution method to the output of the TeleSABRE algorithm. For both approaches, we estimate the cost of handling nonlocal two-qubit gates across a fixed midpoint or quarter-point partition, reporting Bell-pair/classical-communication costs in teleportation. Across Jordan-Wigner and Bravyi-Kitaev, we find that UpCCD with spin-blocked Jordan-Wigner ordering gives the most favorable scaling, while UCCSD incurs substantially larger distributed-resource requirements.
tldr: Estimates teleportation-based distributed quantum computing resource overhead for UCC quantum chemistry ansatze, finding UpCCD with spin-blocked Jordan-Wigner ordering most efficient.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing may help scale quantum chemistry applications beyond monolithic processors, but the communication overhead for nonlocal gates must be quantified.
method: Compares a naive distribution method to the TeleSABRE algorithm for UCCSD, UpCCD, and UpCCGSD circuits on hydrogen chains under midpoint or quarter-point partitions, counting Bell-pair and classical-communication costs across Jordan-Wigner and Bravyi-Kitaev mappings.
result: UpCCD with spin-blocked Jordan-Wigner ordering gives the most favorable scaling, while UCCSD incurs substantially larger distributed-resource requirements.
conclusion: The choice of ansatz, fermion-to-qubit mapping, and circuit distribution method strongly affects the distributed resource requirements of quantum chemistry circuits on teleportation-based DQC architectures.

title: Degree Balance As A Fine-Grained Complexity Boundary For Quantum Sat
authors: Atsuya Hasegawa, Jonas Kamminga, Fran\c{c}ois Le Gall, Suguru Tamaki
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The local Hamiltonian problem is the canonical [MATH]-complete problem, and [MATH] time classical algorithms and [MATH] time quantum algorithms are known to solve the problem in the worst case. It is not clear how to improve these brute force strategies for a broad class of the problem because ground states are highly entangled in general, and we cannot directly apply known strategies for classical CSPs. In this work, we present exponentially faster classical and quantum algorithms under two mild assumptions: (1) the Hamiltonian is frustration-free on YES instances, and (2) it is approximately regular, meaning that every qubit is acted upon by approximately the same number of constraints. We complement these upper bounds by showing that, assuming (Q)SETH, quantum 5-SAT admits no non-trivial worst-case speedup. Our lower bound further demonstrates that the dependence of our algorithms on regularity is in some sense nearly optimal. Specifically, quantum 5-SAT remains (Q)SETH-hard even for Hamiltonians in which all but [MATH] qubits participate in only constantly many constraints, while the remaining [MATH] qubits each participate in [MATH] constraints. By contrast, if either the size of this high-degree subset or the degrees of its qubits is reduced by a factor of [MATH], for any [MATH], our algorithm solves the problem in time [MATH] for some [MATH]. Together, our upper and lower bounds establish a fine-grained complexity dichotomy for quantum satisfiability.
tldr: The paper establishes exponentially faster classical and quantum algorithms for frustration-free, approximately regular local Hamiltonian instances, complemented by (Q)SETH-based lower bounds yielding a fine-grained complexity dichotomy for quantum 5-SAT.
motivation: Brute-force classical O(2^n) and quantum O(2^{n/2}) algorithms for the local Hamiltonian problem are hard to improve because general ground states are highly entangled, blocking standard classical CSP techniques.
method: Under assumptions of frustration-freeness on YES instances and approximate regularity of constraint degrees, the authors design improved classical and quantum algorithms, and prove conditional lower bounds based on (Quantum) Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
result: They obtain exponentially faster algorithms for regular frustration-free instances, and show quantum 5-SAT remains (Q)SETH-hard even for nearly regular Hamiltonians with a small high-degree subset, proving the regularity dependence is nearly optimal.
conclusion: Together the upper and lower bounds give a fine-grained complexity dichotomy for quantum satisfiability, delineating when regularity assumptions enable nontrivial speedups.

title: Improved Quantum Algorithms For Black-Box Abelian Group Decomposition
authors: Junrong Luo, Yinan Li, Francois Le Gall
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decomposing finite Abelian black-box groups into cyclic factors is a basic problem in quantum computation. We give a quantum algorithm for decomposing finite Abelian black-box groups by adapting the quantum sampling and classical lattice-reduction method of Regev's factoring algorithm. The algorithm computes an invariant-factor decomposition and corresponding cyclic generators with high probability. For a group G of order at most 2^n with unique encodings and reversible group-operation cost T_op = Omega(sqrt(n)), our algorithm uses O(sqrt(n)) quantum circuits, each with O~(n T_op) gates and executed at most O(n) times. For comparison, we consider the Cheung-Mosca algorithm, which decomposes the Sylow p-subgroups separately. We also consider the common-modulus implementation of the extended Cheung-Mosca algorithm. Our algorithm reduces the sum of the circuit gate counts from O~(n^2 T_op) to O~(n^(3/2) T_op). The total quantum time bound decreases from O~(n^3 T_op) to O~(n^(5/2) T_op), and the quantum space bound decreases from O(n^2) to O(n) qubits. The classical computation uses polynomially many bit operations and group-operation queries. These improvements rely on two technical ingredients. We prove that the integer relation lattices used in our algorithm admit, with high probability, integral bases whose vectors have Euclidean norm at most exp(O(sqrt(n))). We preserve the circuit-size advantage of Regev's algorithm for group decomposition by incorporating all O(n) sampled generators while keeping the lattice-reduction dimension at O(sqrt(n)).
tldr: A quantum algorithm based on Regev's sampling and lattice-reduction approach that decomposes finite Abelian black-box groups into invariant factors with improved gate-count, time, and qubit-space bounds over Cheung-Mosca type algorithms.
motivation: Decomposing finite Abelian black-box groups into cyclic factors is a fundamental problem in quantum computation, and existing algorithms (Cheung-Mosca, extended versions) are costly in circuit gate count, total quantum time, and qubit space.
method: The authors adapt Regev's quantum sampling plus classical lattice-reduction method for factoring, retaining all O(n) sampled generators while keeping the lattice-reduction dimension at O(sqrt(n)), and prove that the integer relation lattices admit short integral bases with vectors of norm exp(O(sqrt(n))).
result: For groups of order at most 2^n with reversible group-operation cost Omega(sqrt(n)), the algorithm reduces summed circuit gate counts from O~(n^2 T_op) to O~(n^{3/2} T_op), total quantum time from O~(n^3 T_op) to O~(n^{5/2} T_op), and quantum space from O(n^2) to O(n) qubits.
conclusion: The work yields asymptotically better quantum algorithms for Abelian group decomposition, showing that Regev-style lattice techniques extend beyond factoring to black-box group structure problems.

title: Mode-selective Acousto-electric Modulation Of Phonons In A Silicon Photonic Platform
authors: Ruoyu Yuan, Yishu Zhou, Matthew J. Storey, Ryan O. Behunin, Haotian Cheng, Betul Sen, Andrew L. Starbuck, Douglas C. Trotter, Andrew L. Leenheer, Matt Eichenfield, Nils T. Otterstrom, Peter T. Rakich
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Acousto-electric (AE) interactions enable electrical control of acoustic propagation through piezoelectric media. Bringing AE control onto integrated photonic platforms provides a powerful on-chip control mechanism to reconfigure both the acoustic propagation through piezoelectric media. Bringing AE control onto integrated photonic platforms provides a powerful on-chip control mechanism to reconfigure both the acoustic delay line response and the effective photon-phonon interaction by electrically tuning the phonon propagation. Here we report a mode-selective AE modulation effect in a scalable aluminum nitride on silicon-on-insulator (AlN-on-SOI) platform. An applied DC field is seen to modulate the phonon dissipation via changes in carrier concentration in a mode-selective fashion, producing up to 20 dB forward transmission suppression of non-fundamental modes within an acoustic delay line while maintaining the fundamental Rayleigh mode, a phenomenon not captured by conventional AE treatments. To probe these dynamics, we integrate an optical waveguide along the acoustic delay line, providing a broadband, non-destructive interface between the acoustic and optical domains. Leveraging both this optical interface and the underlying mode selectivity, we demonstrate proof-of-concept multi-domain transduction and Rayleigh-mode filtering on this hybrid platform, outlining a scalable path toward electrically reconfigurable mode engineering and microwave-photonic functionality.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a mode-selective acousto-electric modulation effect on an AlN-on-SOI hybrid photonic platform, where a DC field selectively suppresses non-fundamental phonon modes in an acoustic delay line while preserving the fundamental Rayleigh mode.
motivation: Acousto-electric (AE) interactions allow electrical control of acoustic propagation in piezoelectric media, and bringing this control onto integrated photonic platforms could enable reconfigurable acoustic delay lines and tunable photon-phonon interactions.
method: The authors integrate an optical waveguide alongside an acoustic delay line on a scalable AlN-on-SOI platform to provide a broadband, non-destructive acoustic-optical probe, then apply a DC electric field to modulate phonon dissipation via changes in carrier concentration.
result: Up to 20 dB forward transmission suppression of non-fundamental acoustic modes is achieved while the fundamental Rayleigh mode is maintained, a mode-selective behavior not captured by conventional AE treatments; proof-of-concept multi-domain transduction and Rayleigh-mode filtering are demonstrated.
conclusion: The work outlines a scalable route toward electrically reconfigurable phonon mode engineering and microwave-photonic functionality, though the demonstration remains classical and is not benchmarked at the quantum level.

title: Spectral Methods For The Complexity Of Planar Graph Homomorphisms
authors: Ashwin Maran, Jin-Yi Cai, Zhuxiao Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We explore the frontier beyond the recently discovered barrier represented by the [MATH] in the classification theory of planar graph homomorphisms [MATH]. We show that analyzing the spectral relations of [MATH] can prove \#P-hardness when traditional vertex separation and domain-reduction methods with planar edge gadgets provably fail due to the [MATH] barrier. We prove two criteria of \#P-hardness for [MATH]: a spectral criterion and a determinant criterion. It is known that the core problem for the classification of [MATH] for nonnegative matrices [MATH] is for positive definite entry-wise positive matrices. We use the spectral criterion to show that [MATH] is \#P-hard for all circulant matrices of prime order [MATH], while for [MATH] it is precisely the matchgate case and is P-time computable by the FKT algorithm (for planar perfect matching). We also prove a complexity dichotomy for [MATH] problems defined by tensor products of 2 by 2 matrices. This gives a complete complexity classification for this class of matrices, and the FKT algorithm together with a holographic transformation is ---every [MATH] is either (1) P-time computable over all graphs, or (2) \#P-hard in general but P-time computable over planar graphs, or (3) \#P-hard over planar graphs; furthermore, [MATH] in (2) consists of precisely those computable by FKT with a holographic transformation.
tldr: The paper develops spectral and determinant criteria to prove #P-hardness for planar graph homomorphism problems beyond the known barrier, yielding complexity dichotomies for circulant matrices and tensor products of 2x2 matrices.
motivation: Classification theory of planar graph homomorphisms had hit a barrier where traditional vertex-separation and domain-reduction methods with planar edge gadgets provably fail, so new tools are needed.
method: The authors analyze spectral relations of the underlying constraint matrices to derive a spectral criterion and a determinant criterion for #P-hardness, and apply them to circulant matrices of prime order and to tensor products of 2x2 matrices.
result: They show #P-hardness for all circulant matrices of prime order, identify the matchgate case as P-time computable via the FKT algorithm for planar perfect matching, and prove a complete complexity trichotomy for products of 2x2 matrices.
conclusion: The work extends holographic-algorithm-style classification to new matrix classes, but remains a classical complexity-theoretic result with only indirect ties to quantum information.

title: Quantum Computing For Network Security Classification: Near-Term Classification And Long-Term Memory Efficiency
authors: Yuqing Li, Poonam Bala Nehru, Yunpeng Zhang, Danindu Gammanpilage, Xin Jin, Zeguan Wu, Junyu Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing has already been explored in several network-security applications. However, how quantum computing may contribute to network-security classification in both the near term and the longer term has not been systematically discussed. This paper studies this question through two complementary experiments. First, we evaluate near-term quantum-kernel support vector machines (SVMs) on practical network-security classification tasks and compare them with classical SVM baselines on KDD Cup 1999, CICIDS2017, and BoT-IoT. Across these runs, quantum kernels are competitive. They can match or improve classical baselines in some settings, while classical RBF kernels remain stronger in others. This suggests that near-term quantum-kernel methods should be evaluated as practical, dataset-dependent alternatives to classical kernels rather than as uniformly superior replacements. Second, we use quantum oracle sketching (QOS) to study a longer-term memory advantage for classification with streaming classical samples. In QOS, samples are processed online and used to incrementally construct an approximate quantum oracle, which provides coherent query access for downstream quantum algorithms without retaining the entire dataset. Under the QOS-inspired machine-size estimate, comparable accuracy corresponds to a substantially smaller effective memory-size proxy than explicit sparse/QRAM-style storage. Compared with a simple streaming proxy, the result is more nuanced because aggressive feature filtering can make the streaming dimension small. This suggests that the long-term value of quantum computing for network-security classification may lie in memory-efficient data access rather than immediate runtime speedup. Together, these experiments show how quantum computing may contribute to network-security classification from near-term classification performance and longer-term memory efficiency.
tldr: This paper evaluates near-term quantum-kernel SVMs and a long-term quantum oracle sketching approach for network-security classification, finding competitive but dataset-dependent performance and potential memory-efficiency advantages.
motivation: To systematically assess how quantum computing can contribute to network-security classification in both the near term and the longer term.
method: Near-term quantum-kernel SVMs are compared with classical SVM baselines on KDD Cup 1999, CICIDS2017, and BoT-IoT; additionally, quantum oracle sketching (QOS) is used to process streaming classical samples and incrementally construct an approximate quantum oracle for coherent query access without retaining the full dataset.
result: Quantum kernels can match or improve classical baselines in some settings but remain dataset-dependent, while QOS suggests a substantially smaller effective memory-size proxy than explicit sparse/QRAM-style storage, though aggressive feature filtering can reduce the streaming dimension and nuance the advantage.
conclusion: Near-term quantum-kernel methods should be viewed as practical, dataset-dependent alternatives rather than uniformly superior replacements; the long-term value of quantum computing for network-security classification may lie in memory-efficient data access rather than immediate runtime speedup.

title: Ldpc Fractus Codes: Sparse Codes With Recursive Structure
authors: Jes\'us Carrillo-Pacheco
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new family of recursively constructed sparse matrices, termed Fractus matrices, and investigate their use in constructing low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Generated through a self-similar recursive process, these matrices yield regular sparse parity-check matrices while preserving key structural properties across successive iterations. This recursive structure enables an efficient encoding algorithm with computational complexity that is nearly linear in the block length. Decoding is performed using standard iterative message-passing algorithms, thereby retaining the low-complexity decoding characteristic of LDPC codes. The proposed construction produces Tanner graphs with girth six and guarantees a minimum Hamming distance of at least [MATH]. We establish several algebraic properties of Fractus matrices, including sparsity, regularity, recursive decomposition, and symmetry under the flip-transpose operation. In addition, we show that the family of Fractus matrices admits a natural lattice structure and that the associated LDPC codes inherit corresponding lattice-theoretic properties. These results establish a connection between order theory and coding theory. Overall, the proposed framework integrates recursive matrix constructions, efficient encoding, graph-theoretic analysis, and lattice theory into a unified algebraic approach to the design and analysis of scalable LDPC codes.
tldr: Introduces Fractus matrices, a recursively constructed family of sparse matrices, and uses them to build LDPC codes with efficient encoding and girth-six Tanner graphs.
motivation: To design scalable LDPC codes with low-complexity encoding/decoding and algebraic structure that connects order theory and coding theory.
method: Defines self-similar recursive Fractus matrices, analyzes their sparsity, regularity, recursive decomposition, flip-transpose symmetry, and lattice structure, then constructs LDPC codes decoded via standard message-passing.
result: The construction yields regular sparse parity-check matrices, girth-six Tanner graphs, a minimum Hamming distance lower bound, nearly linear encoding complexity, and lattice-theoretic properties.
conclusion: Provides a unified algebraic framework for scalable LDPC code design, but remains within classical coding theory with no quantum extension.

title: On The Capacity Of Dna Labeling In The Single-Label Setting
authors: Zihan Wu, Qi Cao, Ling Liu, Baoming Bai
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DNA labeling has attracted increasing attention in biomedical applications, including molecular imaging, diagnostics, and genomic analysis. In a DNA labeling process, a set of DNA sequence patterns, referred to as labels, is designed according to the requirements of a specific application. For each DNA sequence, the labeling process generates an output sequence that records the positions of the labels. DNA sequences with different labeling outputs can therefore be distinguished through the labeling process. To quantify this capability, the labeling capacity is defined as the exponential growth rate of the maximum number of DNA sequences that can be distinguished through the labeling process as the sequence length tends to infinity [2]. To date, the labeling capacities of several cases in the single-label setting have been determined. In this paper, we formulate the labeling process as a deterministic channel and show that its zero-error capacity is equal to the labeling capacity. For a single label, the corresponding channel can be represented by a star graph. Thus, characterizing the labeling capacity of a single label is equivalent to determining the zero-error capacity of the corresponding star graph. We derive the zero-error capacities of all star graphs, thereby providing a complete characterization of the labeling capacities for all single-label cases. Furthermore, we develop a general method for constructing capacity-achieving codes. These results apply to labeling problems over arbitrary finite alphabets and are not restricted to the DNA alphabet. Finally, for a fixed label length, we exactly characterize the range of achievable labeling capacities and identify all single-label structures that attain the minimum and maximum capacities.
tldr: The paper models DNA labeling as a deterministic channel and completely determines the zero-error capacity of all star graphs, thereby fully characterizing single-label DNA labeling capacities over arbitrary finite alphabets.
motivation: DNA labeling is increasingly used to distinguish DNA sequences in biomedical applications, and the labeling capacity quantifies the exponential growth of distinguishable sequences, but only limited single-label cases were previously solved.
method: The labeling process is formulated as a deterministic channel whose zero-error capacity equals the labeling capacity; for a single label the channel reduces to a star graph, and the zero-error capacities of all star graphs are derived, along with a general capacity-achieving code construction.
result: The work provides a complete characterization of labeling capacities for all single-label cases, characterizes the exact range of achievable capacities for fixed label length, and identifies the label structures attaining minimum and maximum capacities.
conclusion: These results offer a rigorous information-theoretic foundation for DNA labeling and enable the design of capacity-achieving codes, extending beyond the standard DNA alphabet to arbitrary finite alphabets.

title: Memory-induced Optimal Switching In A Dynamic Ising-Kuramoto Model
authors: Reon Hayashi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a globally coupled stochastic system in which each unit carries an Ising spin and a continuous phase. The spins undergo Glauber switching with relaxation rate [MATH], while the phases are driven by Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise with correlation time [MATH]. A spin-dependent phase interaction supports a composite coherent mode, [MATH], that can order even when the ordinary phase coherence is small. Linear response about the nonmagnetic incoherent state gives the synchronization threshold [MATH], where [MATH] is a memory-weighted Laplace transform of the free phase correlation function. The competition between the increasing Glauber response and the decreasing memory susceptibility produces a finite switching rate at which [MATH] is minimized.
