These gains persist under a fixed LLM backbone in our evaluation. ANCHOR processes a full audit day at dollar-level API cost, supporting practical, context-grounded investigation across windows.
tldr: ANCHOR is an investigation-oriented system provenance framework that pairs curated evidence queues with context-grounded, stateful LLM reasoning to reconstruct multi-stage attack narratives from audit streams.
motivation: Provenance-based intrusion detection systems flag suspicious activity but struggle to convert local anomalous subgraphs into coherent attack narratives, since direct LLM analysis lacks deployment-specific normal-behavior knowledge and validated attack state across temporally dispersed evidence.
method: ANCHOR calibrates anomaly judgments by relation type, links anomalous windows via rare relation-role patterns to build causally structured evidence queues, and uses Deployment Context (environment baselines plus high-risk security knowledge) and Case Context (a confidence-gated Attack-Tracking Cache) to incrementally interpret process-centered evidence.
result: Evaluated on six DARPA Transparent Computing E3/E5 datasets across three operating systems, ANCHOR improved overall indicator-of-compromise recovery and kill-chain stage attribution over state-of-the-art provenance baselines under a fixed LLM backbone, at dollar-level API cost per full audit day.
conclusion: Context-grounded, stateful LLM reasoning over curated provenance evidence enables practical, scalable attack investigation, though the work lies entirely in systems security rather than quantum information science.

title: What Do City Codes Say About Climate Risk?
authors: Arianna Salazar-Miranda
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Climate change is intensifying natural hazards, and preparing cities for them falls primarily to local governments. Yet what municipal codes say about hazards, and whether their requirements match each city's risk profile, has not been measured. I analyze 3.6 million sentences from 204 U.S. cities' municipal codes and compare each city's hazard text to its actual risk from FEMA's National Risk Index. I document four patterns. First, a small share of code text consists of provisions relevant for natural hazards (1.5%), and codes in high-risk cities contain marginally more. Second, hazard coverage is highly concentrated on flooding (61% of hazard-relevant text), even though flooding accounts for only 9% of the average city's risk. Third, city codes emphasize emergency response over prevention. Emergency management is the largest regulatory category, and land use is the smallest. Fourth, codes track the types of risks relevant to each location, but only loosely. The median city would need to reallocate 70% of its regulatory text to match its risk profile. The results suggest that U.S. city codes do not include regulation for most of the hazards cities face.
tldr: An analysis of 3.6 million sentences from 204 U.S. municipal codes shows that city regulations on natural hazards are sparse, heavily flood-focused, response-oriented, and only loosely matched to each city's actual FEMA risk profile.
motivation: Climate change is intensifying natural hazards, and local governments bear primary responsibility for preparedness, yet no systematic measurement existed of what municipal codes actually say about hazards or whether they align with local risk.
method: The author extracts and classifies hazard-relevant sentences from the municipal codes of 204 U.S. cities and compares the resulting hazard-topic distribution against each city's risk composition from FEMA's National Risk Index.
result: Only 1.5% of code text concerns natural hazards, with 61% of that focused on flooding despite flooding being only 9% of average risk; emergency response dominates over prevention, and the median city would need to reallocate 70% of its regulatory text to match its risk profile.
conclusion: U.S. municipal codes regulate only a small and poorly matched fraction of the hazards cities face, suggesting a substantial gap between local climate risk and local regulatory preparedness.

title: Derivation Of The General Solution Of The Black-Scholes Boundary-Value Problem
authors: M. Y. Choi Byoungseon Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There are infinitely many functions that satisfy the Black-Scholes partial differential equation and the terminal condition corresponding to the European call option. This means that the Black-Scholes formula, which led to the award of the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, is not the unique solution, as was once assumed. Consequently, it violates the law of one price, one of the fundamental laws of economics and finance. In this article, we present a rigorous derivation of these solutions to the Black-Scholes boundary value problem.
tldr: The paper rigorously derives the full family of solutions to the Black-Scholes boundary-value problem, showing the celebrated Black-Scholes formula is not unique.
motivation: The authors observe that infinitely many functions satisfy the Black-Scholes PDE with the European call terminal condition, implying the standard pricing formula violates the law of one price.
method: A rigorous mathematical derivation of the general solution to the Black-Scholes boundary-value problem is presented, characterizing all admissible solutions.
result: The derivation yields a broader solution class than the classical Black-Scholes formula, demonstrating non-uniqueness of option prices under the given boundary conditions.
conclusion: The findings challenge the uniqueness assumption underlying the Black-Scholes pricing framework and have implications for economic no-arbitrage principles.

title: Slip Wall Boundary Conditions In Curved Domains For Finite Element Ale Hydrodynamics
authors: Nabil Atallah, Kevin Sweet, Paul Moujaes, Jan Nikl, Ketan Mittal, Vladimir Z. Tomov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a high-order finite element arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) method for hydrodynamics with slip-wall boundary conditions on analytically curved domains. The method combines distinct Lagrangian, remesh, and remap phases while preserving the geometric features of curved boundaries and allowing tangential motion of boundary nodes. In the Lagrangian phase, we use weak boundary condition enforcement to impose the slip-wall condition without freezing tangential motion. In the mesh optimization phase, we adapt TMOP (target-matrix optimization paradigm) to analytic walls by replacing selected boundary coordinate degrees of freedom with curve or surface parameters. The Newton solve then moves boundary nodes tangentially with respect to the prescribed geometry while carrying the drift introduced by the Lagrangian phase. In the remap phase, we transfer the solution from the old mesh to the optimized mesh by a conservative advection-based remap over pseudo-time. We present numerical results in two and three dimensions demonstrating the method on high-order curved meshes and showing that it preserves boundary fidelity while producing the expected hydrodynamic solution features.
tldr: A high-order finite element arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) hydrodynamics method that enforces slip-wall boundary conditions on analytically curved domains while allowing tangential motion of boundary nodes.
motivation: Accurate treatment of curved boundaries is essential for high-order hydrodynamic simulations, yet standard slip-wall conditions often freeze tangential node motion or degrade geometric fidelity on curved meshes.
method: The scheme separates Lagrangian, remesh, and remap phases: weak (variational) enforcement of the slip-wall condition in the Lagrangian phase, TMOP-based mesh optimization that replaces boundary coordinate degrees of freedom with curve/surface parameters, and a conservative advection-based remap over pseudo-time.
result: Two- and three-dimensional numerical experiments on high-order curved meshes show preserved boundary fidelity and the expected hydrodynamic solution features, including tangential node motion carrying Lagrangian drift.
conclusion: The method offers a robust, geometrically faithful approach to slip-wall ALE hydrodynamics on curved domains, though the work is purely classical computational fluid dynamics with no quantum information or thermodynamic content.

title: Asymptotic Rigidity And Boundary Structure Of Yang's Numerical Invariants For The Bidisk Submodules $[z^k-w^\ell]$
authors: Yin Liu, Yufeng Lu, Yixin Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let \[ M_{k,\ell}=[z^k-w^\ell]\subset H^2(\mathbb D^2), \qquad k,\ell\in\mathbb N,\quad k\ne\ell . \] We study the large-index asymptotics of Yang's numerical invariants and the boundary structure of their generating function. Starting from the exact staircase formula obtained in our preceding work, we prove that \[ \Sigma_j(M_{k,\ell}) = }{j} + O(j^{-2}), \] where \[ C_{k,\ell} = \int_0^\infty {(x+1/k)^2(x+1/\ell)^2}\,dx . \] The first strict descent together with [MATH] recovers the unordered pair [MATH], yielding an asymptotic rigidity principle. At the next order we obtain a periodic correction \[ \Sigma_j(M_{k,\ell}) = }{j} + (j)}{j^2} + O(j^{-3}), \] whose least period is \((k,\ell)\), and we determine the leading amplitudes of the strict drops. For Yang's generating function \[ \mathcal P_{k,\ell}(t) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\Sigma_j(M_{k,\ell})t^j, \] we prove that it has radius of convergence one and a logarithmic singularity at [MATH]; hence it is never a polynomial for [MATH], giving a negative answer to Yang's polynomiality question within this quasi-homogeneous family. The periodic higher-order corrections generate root-of-unity polylogarithmic boundary modes. The leading logarithmic coefficient together with the second-order boundary support determines the unordered pair [MATH], while successive renormalized boundary limits recover the Fourier coefficients of every finite-order periodic asymptotic term.
tldr: The paper studies the large-index asymptotics and boundary behavior of Yang's numerical invariants for a quasi-homogeneous family of bidisk submodules [z^k - w^l] in H^2(D^2), proving an asymptotic rigidity principle and answering Yang's polynomiality question negatively.
motivation: Yang's numerical invariants are index-theoretic quantities for submodules of the bidisk Hardy space that encode structural information about the submodule, and their asymptotic behavior was previously known only through an exact staircase formula.
method: Starting from the exact staircase formula, the authors perform asymptotic analysis of the invariant series, derive a periodic correction at second order, and analyze the generating function's radius of convergence and singularity structure using polylogarithmic boundary modes.
result: They prove Sigma_j = C/j + O(1/j^2) with an explicit integral constant C_{k,l}, establish a period-(k,l) second-order correction, and show the generating function has radius one with a logarithmic singularity, so it is never polynomial and boundary modes recover Fourier coefficients and the unordered pair {k,l}.
conclusion: The results establish an asymptotic rigidity principle for these bidisk submodules and give a negative answer to Yang's polynomiality question within this quasi-homogeneous family.

title: Second-Moment Stochastic Approximation Methods
authors: Lin Xiao Tao Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical stochastic approximation methods rely on estimators of the first moment (mean) of a random regression function. We study methods that employ estimators of both the first and the second moments, which include modern deep-learning optimizers such as Adam and Muon as special cases. We derive second-moment stochastic approximation methods through the lens of optimal preconditioning for solving matrix equations, and develop a two-stage framework for their convergence analysis. The first stage focuses on the analysis of conceptual (impractical) methods that rely on the exact first and second moments. In the second stage, we replace the exact moments with their respective estimators, and invoke Dvoretzky's theorem to show that the resulting practical methods converge almost surely to a neighborhood of the target solution. The size of the neighborhood depends on the biases and variances of the first- and second-moment estimators. We derive concrete bounds for Muon and a spectral variant of Adam that determine the radius of their neighborhood of convergence.
tldr: This paper develops second-moment stochastic approximation methods, including Adam and Muon as special cases, with convergence analysis based on optimal preconditioning and Dvoretzky's theorem.
motivation: Classical stochastic approximation relies only on first-moment estimators, but modern deep-learning optimizers use both first and second moments; the authors aim to provide a unified theoretical framework for such methods.
method: They derive second-moment methods via optimal preconditioning for matrix equations and use a two-stage analysis: first for conceptual methods with exact moments, then for practical methods with estimators via Dvoretzky's theorem.
result: They obtain almost-sure convergence to a neighborhood whose size depends on estimator biases and variances, with concrete bounds for Muon and a spectral variant of Adam.
conclusion: The framework explains and bounds the behavior of popular second-moment optimizers, bridging stochastic approximation theory and modern deep-learning optimization.

title: Exact Hill Shares Are Simultaneous Guarantees
authors: Bo Li, Hanyu Li, Chenghua Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fair division of indivisible bads seeks allocations that guarantee every agent a bundle whose cost is no larger than a meaningful fairness benchmark. The canonical minimax share has widely been used; unfortunately, it is not a simultaneous guarantee. Hill (Ann. Probab., 1987) initiated a complementary approach in which the share depends only on the number of agents and the largest possible single-item value. Li et al. (ACM Trans. Econ. Comput., 2024) gave the exact Hill formula and proved that its monotone closure is a simultaneous guarantee. The closure treats the largest-item cost only as an upper bound and can be strictly larger than the share conditioned on the largest item. They asked whether this smaller exact share is itself simultaneously guaranteed for three or more agents. We resolve this open question affirmatively. For any number of agents and arbitrary heterogeneous largest-item costs, there is one allocation that satisfies every agent's exact Hill's share. We further provide a polynomial-time algorithm computes such an allocation. Our algorithm combines an ordered moving knife with a tail-domination invariant, and a one-sided trimmed subset-sum routine for the two-agent endpoint without computing an exact minimax partition.
tldr: The paper resolves an open question in fair division of indivisible bads by proving that the exact Hill share is a simultaneous guarantee for any number of agents and providing a polynomial-time allocation algorithm.
motivation: Fair division of indivisible bads seeks allocations that guarantee each agent a bundle no costlier than a fairness benchmark, but the canonical minimax share is not a simultaneous guarantee.
method: The authors prove the affirmative for the exact Hill share using an ordered moving knife combined with a tail-domination invariant and a one-sided trimmed subset-sum routine for the two-agent endpoint.
result: For any number of agents and arbitrary heterogeneous largest-item costs, a single allocation satisfies every agent's exact Hill share, and such an allocation can be computed in polynomial time.
conclusion: The exact Hill share is indeed simultaneously guaranteed, answering the open question of Li et al. and yielding an efficient constructive algorithm.

title: Full Justified Representation In Temporal Voting: Efficient Computation And Verification
authors: Nicholas Teh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In temporal voting, a fixed set of voters makes a collective decision in each of several rounds, and proportionality requires that groups with shared interests be represented across these decisions. Full justified representation (FJR) is among the strongest proportionality axioms known to be satisfiable in this setting, since it allows different members of a group to be satisfied by different selected candidates. However, whether an FJR outcome can be computed in polynomial time has remained open. We resolve this question by introducing temporal FJR+, a strengthening of both FJR and extended justified representation+ (EJR+) that can be computed and verified in polynomial time. The axiom measures a group's agreement in each round by the largest number of its members who approve a common candidate, and requires some member to attain the integer part of the group's proportional share of its best attainable average satisfaction, with a shortfall of at most one unit when this share is an integer. We show that verification reduces to counting approvals among the voters below each satisfaction threshold. For computation, we observe that local search for Proportional Approval Voting (PAV) can stop at an outcome violating FJR. Somewhat counterintuitively, the remedy is to subtract a small multiple of the minimum voter satisfaction from the PAV score: every FJR+ violation then admits a single-round change whose improvement guarantees polynomial running time. We further show that temporal FJR+ is strictly stronger than FJR and EJR+ combined, and coincides with lower quota on party-list preferences. Finally, temporal FJR+ and multiwinner FJR+ are incomparable in general, but coincide when approvals are static and each candidate-round pair is treated as a separate candidate.
tldr: The paper resolves the computational complexity of Full Justified Representation in temporal voting by introducing a stronger axiom, temporal FJR+, that can be computed and verified in polynomial time.
motivation: Full justified representation (FJR) is a strong proportionality axiom for temporal voting, but whether an FJR outcome can be computed in polynomial time was open.
method: The authors define temporal FJR+, a strengthening of FJR and EJR+, and show verification reduces to counting approvals below satisfaction thresholds; for computation, they modify Proportional Approval Voting by subtracting a small multiple of the minimum voter satisfaction to guarantee polynomial-time local search.
result: Temporal FJR+ is strictly stronger than FJR and EJR+ combined, coincides with lower quota on party-list preferences, and is incomparable with multiwinner FJR+ except when approvals are static and candidate-round pairs are separate candidates.
conclusion: The work resolves the open problem by providing an efficiently computable and verifiable proportionality axiom for temporal voting, with clear axiomatic comparisons to existing notions.

title: SameFact: The Same Safety Facts Lead To Different Responses Across Interfaces
authors: Dongsheng Chen, Jiaxin Zhang, Lei Ma, Xin Yao, Xuetao Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety evaluations often ask whether a model recognizes that an action is unsafe, whereas agent evaluations ask what the model chooses to do. Using safety judgments as evidence about action selection therefore raises a measurement question: does the influence of the same safety-relevant fact persist across response interfaces? We introduce SameFact, a matched-counterfactual benchmark that tests this question directly. SameFact contains 300 safe/unsafe pairs that hold the task, prior observations, candidate action, identifiers, and non-target facts fixed while changing a single state-grounded safety fact. Across six LLM backbones, we measure the effect of this matched intervention through three interfaces at the same candidate-action boundary: explicit safety judgment, checkpoint candidate admission, and open first-action selection. All six backbones show lower aggregate sensitivity under open first-action selection than under judgment, but the change is not a uniform attenuation: across 24 model-factor cells, Spearman agreement falls from 0.817 between judgment and checkpoint admission to 0.470 between judgment and open first-action selection, while pairwise ordering disagreement rises from 18.5% to 32.6%. A follow-up 2x2 first-response experiment shows that a checkpoint-style protocol increases measured sensitivity in all six backbones by 8.4-29.3 percentage points, whereas action-space effects and their interactions with protocol vary in magnitude and direction across models. These results show that the response interface is part of the measured quantity: judgment and action interfaces share safety signal, but do not provide interchangeable measurements of how safety-relevant facts shape model responses.
tldr: SameFact is a matched-counterfactual benchmark showing that the same safety-relevant fact produces different measured effects depending on whether a model is asked to judge safety, admit a candidate action at a checkpoint, or select an open first action.
motivation: Safety evaluations treat safety judgments as evidence about action selection, but it is unclear whether the influence of a given safety fact persists across different response interfaces relevant to agent behaviour.
method: The authors build 300 safe/unsafe pairs holding task, prior observations, candidate action, identifiers, and non-target facts fixed while varying a single state-grounded safety fact, then measure intervention effects across three interfaces in six LLM backbones, plus a 2x2 first-response experiment.
result: Aggregate sensitivity is lower under open first-action selection than under judgment, but not uniformly: Spearman agreement drops from 0.817 (judgment vs checkpoint admission) to 0.470 (judgment vs open first-action selection), and pairwise ordering disagreement rises from 18.5% to 32.6%; a checkpoint-style protocol raises measured sensitivity by 8.4–29.3 percentage points in all six backbones.
conclusion: The response interface is part of the measured quantity: judgment and action interfaces share safety signal but are not interchangeable measurements of how safety-relevant facts shape model responses.

title: MMSkillRisk: Can Agents Stay Safe When Multimodal Skills Become Traps?
authors: Lingqi Jiang, Jialuo Chen, Jianan Ma, Xinhao Deng, Xiaohu Du, Sibo Yi, Yuqi Qing, Zhenguang Liu, Qinming He, Shiwen Cui, Changhua Men
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills are shareable packages of procedural instructions, tools, and examples. Multimodal skills additionally include visual references that agents retrieve and inspect during execution. Because these images guide actions, attackers can disguise malicious instructions as ordinary visual guidance within otherwise legitimate skills. Existing skill-security research primarily examines text-carried attacks or scanner detection, leaving the runtime effects of image-borne attacks insufficiently evaluated. We introduce MMSkillRisk, to our knowledge the first publicly available benchmark dedicated to end-to-end safety evaluation of image-borne attacks in multimodal skills. To instantiate this attack surface, we design Native-Context Visual Attack (NCVA), which disguises malicious instructions as native components of teaching images, such as annotations and interface labels. The accompanying SKILL.md provides auxiliary guidance toward relevant visual regions without explicitly stating the malicious operation. Built from 28 curated clean skills, MMSkillRisk contains 36 attack packages and 108 executable cases spanning five attack objectives, with separate checks for attack success and legitimate-task completion. Across nine model-harness configurations evaluated in isolated sandboxes, NCVA induces unauthorized operations in every configuration. Its pooled attack success rate (ASR) reaches 43.1%, exceeding the matched text-carrier baseline by 16.4 percentage points, with higher ASR in all nine configurations. Attack success and legitimate-task completion co-occur in 36.5% of cases, reaching 72.2% for GPT-5.6-sol with Codex. These results show that skill-bundled images can induce unauthorized actions even as agents complete legitimate tasks, so task success alone does not establish safe skill use. Our code and data are available at [URL].
tldr: MMSkillRisk is a benchmark for evaluating image-borne attacks in multimodal agent skills, showing that malicious visual instructions can induce unauthorized actions while legitimate tasks still complete.
motivation: Agent skills increasingly include visual references, creating a new attack surface where attackers can embed malicious instructions in images rather than text.
method: The authors build a benchmark from 28 clean skills with 36 attack packages and 108 executable cases, and design Native-Context Visual Attack (NCVA) to disguise malicious instructions as native teaching-image components.
result: Across nine model-harness configurations, NCVA achieves a pooled attack success rate of 43.1%, exceeding the text-carrier baseline by 16.4 percentage points, with attack success and legitimate-task completion co-occurring in 36.5% of cases.
conclusion: Task success alone does not establish safe skill use, and image-borne attacks in multimodal skills require dedicated safety evaluation and defenses.

title: When Privacy Becomes A Weapon: Understanding Doxxing And Privacy Vulnerabilities In Mainland China's Social Media Ecosystem
authors: Xiao Zhan, Shijing He, Chi Zhang, Jose Such
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Doxxing, the malicious disclosure of personal information, has become a pervasive privacy threat. Yet existing research remains predominantly Western-centric, limiting our understanding of how doxxing unfolds in contexts where mandatory identity systems, platform governance, and cultural logics fundamentally reshape privacy risks and harm trajectories. We address this gap through semi-structured interviews with 18 doxxing survivors in mainland China, synthesizing their experiences into a framework conceptualizing how doxxing operates in this context. Our findings reveal both patterns echoing prior Western findings, such as platform amplification mechanisms that resonate with Western findings, and China-specific dynamics shaped by the interplay of regulatory mandates (compulsory identity linkage) and cultural logics including nationalist discourse, fandom culture, Confucian values, and low privacy literacy. Survivors' experiences further reveal how doxxing reshapes understanding of privacy: from preference to precondition, from momentary disclosure to temporal vulnerability, and from individual control to structural powerlessness. These insights challenge agency-centered privacy frameworks and suggest that effective protection requires constraining systemic vulnerabilities rather than relying solely on user empowerment. We conclude by proposing multifaceted recommendations spanning legal reform, platform design, and social initiatives.
tldr: A qualitative interview study of 18 doxxing survivors in mainland China that develops a framework for how mandatory identity systems, platform governance, and cultural logics shape privacy harms.
motivation: Existing doxxing research is predominantly Western-centric, leaving gaps in understanding how doxxing operates under mandatory identity systems and distinct cultural and regulatory contexts.
method: Semi-structured interviews with 18 doxxing survivors in mainland China, analyzed to synthesize a conceptual framework of doxxing dynamics in that ecosystem.
result: Findings show both Western-like platform amplification mechanisms and China-specific dynamics driven by compulsory identity linkage, nationalist discourse, fandom culture, Confucian values, and low privacy literacy, reshaping privacy from preference to precondition.
conclusion: The authors argue agency-centered privacy frameworks are inadequate and recommend systemic protections via legal reform, platform design, and social initiatives.

title: Solving The Arctic Product-Mix Auction
authors: Elizabeth Baldwin, Paul Klemperer, Edwin Lock
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Arctic product-mix auctions allow budget-constrained bidders to express preferences over multiple substitute goods. We give the first strongly polynomial algorithm to find the competitive equilibria when the auctioneer has separable convex piecewise-linear costs. It combines a strongly polynomial reduction to the costless Arctic auction with an existing strongly polynomial algorithm for costless Arctic auctions. We also give a polynomial-time Turing reduction from costless Arctic auctions to linear Fisher markets, and a strongly polynomial many-to-one reduction to linear Arrow-Debreu exchange markets. If a good is sold in positive quantity in two competitive equilibria, its price is the same in both.
tldr: The paper presents the first strongly polynomial algorithm for finding competitive equilibria in Arctic product-mix auctions with budget-constrained bidders and separable convex piecewise-linear costs.
motivation: Product-mix auctions allow bidders to express preferences over substitute goods, but computing competitive equilibria under budget constraints and auctioneer costs has been challenging.
method: The authors reduce the Arctic product-mix auction with separable convex piecewise-linear costs to the costless Arctic auction, then use a known strongly polynomial algorithm for the latter, and also relate costless Arctic auctions to linear Fisher and Arrow-Debreu exchange markets.
result: They obtain a strongly polynomial algorithm for the general problem, polynomial-time Turing reductions between Arctic auctions and linear Fisher markets, and a many-to-one reduction to linear Arrow-Debreu exchange markets, plus a uniqueness property for prices of goods sold in positive quantity.
conclusion: The work provides efficient algorithms and complexity reductions for Arctic product-mix auctions, advancing the theory of market equilibrium computation, but it lies outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Audience-Bound Persistent Memory: Authorization Across The Memory Lifecycle
authors: Sibo Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A personal language agent that acts for its owner across private and shared conversations can learn a fact from one audience and later place it in the context it assembles for another. We study authorization before context across the whole memory lifecycle. Each memory item carries the audience present when it was recorded; derived items are partitioned by audience, receive the intersection of their sources' audiences, or are suppressed; an audience widens only by an explicit, object-specific grant; and an item enters a model attempt only when every current viewer belongs to one of its authorized audiences, with unresolved viewers failing closed to public-only. Under explicit identity, provenance and complete-mediation assumptions, this admission is sound and policy-complete on the exact assembled context, enforced by exclusion rather than by model behavior. We realize it in two independently persisted reference architectures, a flat store and a relationship graph, and, descriptively, in a native agent-memory runtime. In a prospectively frozen confirmation over 10,000 multi-party histories, no forbidden item entered any architecture's context, whereas unscoped retrieval exposed forbidden items in 82% of its contexts. Entitled recall matched policy-equivalent baselines exactly and exceeded unscoped retrieval by 0.30 Recall@5, with a Holm-confirmed advantage that grows with distractors. No architecture produced a wrong-principal substitution, but unscoped substitutions were too rare to establish the prespecified joint decision.
tldr: The paper studies authorization for persistent memory in personal language agents by binding each memory item to the audience present when it was recorded and enforcing audience-based access across the memory lifecycle.
motivation: Personal language agents can learn facts in one private or shared conversation and improperly reuse them in another audience's context, creating a need for authorization before context assembly.
method: The author formalizes audience-bound memory admission under explicit identity, provenance, and complete-mediation assumptions, with derived-item audience partitioning, intersection, suppression, and explicit widening grants; it is realized in flat-store and relationship-graph reference architectures and tested over 10,000 multi-party histories.
result: No forbidden item entered any architecture's context under the proposed admission control, while unscoped retrieval exposed forbidden items in 82% of contexts; entitled recall matched policy-equivalent baselines and exceeded unscoped retrieval by 0.30 Recall@5.
conclusion: Audience-bound persistent memory provides sound and policy-complete authorization on the assembled context, enforced by exclusion rather than model behavior, though wrong-principal substitution effects were too rare to establish the prespecified joint decision.

title: A Density Deficit For Sums Of Three Cube-full Numbers
authors: Basile Beyer de Ryke
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be the set of positive cube-full integers. We prove that, for every [MATH], there is a reduced residue class in which [MATH] has upper relative density at most [MATH]. Consequently, the positive integers not representable as sums of at most three cube-full numbers have positive lower natural density. This proves the infinitude assertion in Erds Problem \#940 for [MATH]. The argument combines a cubic-character estimate with a truncation of the parametrisation by the canonical 4-full part.
tldr: The paper proves a density-deficit result for sums of at most three cube-full numbers, resolving the infinitude part of Erdős Problem #940 via cubic-character estimates.
motivation: Erdős Problem #940 asks about the structure of integers representable as sums of few cube-full numbers, a purely classical additive number theory question.
method: The author combines a cubic-character (Dirichlet L-function) estimate with a truncation of the parametrization of cube-full integers by their canonical 4-full part, to bound upper relative density in a reduced residue class.
result: For every prescribed bound, there exists a reduced residue class in which the set of cube-full integers has upper relative density at most a small constant, implying the non-representable integers have positive lower natural density.
conclusion: The infinitude assertion of Erdős Problem #940 for three cube-full numbers is established, advancing classical additive number theory.

title: Same Bytes, Different Authority: Reserved-Token Representations In Chat-Template Prompt Injection
authors: Yan Zhan, Yunze Song, Mengkai Hou, Wanting Zhang, Shaobo Liu, Zhijun Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.35932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt injection against LLM agents becomes much stronger when the injected instruction is wrapped in the model's own chat template. A forged template marker such as <|im_start|> can reach the model either as a single reserved control token or as a sequence of ordinary subword tokens. The two decode to exactly the same text, and because tokenization runs on the server, the defender rather than the attacker decides which one the model receives. We use this to measure how much of the injected instruction's authority comes from the reserved token's learned representation. Encoding the forged markers as subwords, with the text held fixed and a control for the extra tokens this adds, lowers attack success on the InjecAgent benchmark by 39 to 66 percentage points on three of four open-weight families, and the gap carries over to multi-turn agent tasks in AgentDojo. On Qwen3-8B the gap is 8 points, because without reserved ids the model still recognises the forged turn from its text by reasoning; suppressing the reasoning block widens the gap to 50. The authority sits in the single learned vector at the marker position: the mean of the marker's subword vectors does not reproduce it, the vector of the nearest ordinary token restores the attack on Llama-3.1, and an adaptive attacker who searches for non-reserved markers finds such embedding neighbours on three of four families. In every base and instruction-tuned pair we test, instruction tuning strengthens the model's preference for reserved markers. The standard mitigation, a tokenizer option that encodes special tokens as ordinary subwords, applies only to tokens a configuration declares special, so in 33 of 67 distinct tokenizer configurations, covering 255 of the 400 most-downloaded chat models on Hugging Face, it leaves intact the tool-protocol tokens through which agents read untrusted tool output, and the gap persists on that channel.
tldr: The paper studies how reserved-token representations in chat templates amplify prompt injection attacks against LLM agents, and how tokenization choices affect attack success.
motivation: Prompt injection becomes more dangerous when forged chat-template markers are encoded as reserved control tokens rather than ordinary subwords, yet tokenization is controlled by the defender/server.
method: The authors compare attack success when forged template markers are encoded as reserved tokens versus subword sequences, controlling for added tokens, across multiple open-weight model families and benchmarks like InjecAgent and AgentDojo.
result: Subword encoding lowers attack success by 39–66 percentage points on three of four families, with smaller gaps on Qwen3-8B that widen when reasoning is suppressed; the authority is tied to the learned marker vector, not the text alone.
conclusion: Defenses must account for reserved token representations in chat templates, as standard special-token handling leaves many tool-protocol tokens unprotected and allows prompt injection to persist.

title: Fast Hamiltonian Engineering From Cut Polytope Geometry
authors: Thomas Joachim Friese, \"ozg\"un Kum, Aram W. Harrow, Martin Kliesch
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hamiltonian engineering (HE) simulates quantum dynamics under a target Hamiltonian using a native entangling system Hamiltonian and restricted control, with applications from quantum gate design to analog quantum simulation. Observing that, for many systems, formulating HE as a linear program only requires specific commutation relations between the control pulses and the system Hamiltonian, we provide a unified framework for broad classes of [MATH]-local qubit, qudit, and fermionic systems. We reformulate time-optimal HE as a complex [MATH]-cut polytope problem, with [MATH] the number of distinct phases in these commutation relations, and prove it NP-complete for every finite [MATH]. We therefore relax the polytope to the elliptope and apply a Krivine-type rounding, yielding pulses informed by the system and target Hamiltonians, which we then use in a linear program. We derive how many informed pulses are necessary and sufficient for the linear program to be reliably feasible. Additionally mixing in uniformly sampled pulses guarantees a solution close to the relaxation value from [MATH] pulses, with [MATH] the number of interaction terms. Together with upper and lower bounds on the optimal quantum run time, this yields an [MATH] approximation ratio. In benchmarks on a fully connected Ising model, a chiral clock model for qudits, and the fermionic Harper-Hofstadter model, our approach attains near-optimal quantum run times wherever the optimum is computable, reaches run times that saturate with the lattice size in the fermionic case, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods with [MATH] pulses. This establishes a unified approach with provable guarantees to the automatic programming of analog quantum simulators.
tldr: Analysis failed: LLM returned empty content

title: Permeability And Microcrack Geometry: Dynamic Loading Induced Evolution
authors: Efrem Vitali Rigoberto Moncada
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a crack-geometry-based model for permeability evolution in rocks under dynamic loading. Accurate representation of permeability is important for fluid extraction and containment in geological formations, but remains challenging because low-porosity brittle rocks are highly sensitive to changes in pore geometry and connectivity, while dynamic permeability measurements are limited. Rock void space is represented as an evolving network of penny-shaped cracks with prescribed orientations. Permeability changes are described through crack microvariables including aperture, length, and crack distance. The model accounts for crack opening and closure, fracture-energy-driven propagation, plastic-strain-driven nucleation, coalescence after full connectivity is reached, and strain-rate-dependent fracture toughening. The evolving crack network directly modifies connectivity, fluid conductance, and preferential flow paths. The formulation is implemented in the GeoDyn hydrocode and evaluated under tension, shear, compression, and symmetric impact loading. Results show a strong relation between permeability and crack length, with crack propagation playing a major role in permeability enhancement. Permeability growth can nevertheless be limited by poor connectivity and crack closure. The model captures changes of several orders of magnitude depending on stress state, strain rate, crack orientation, and connectivity, consistent with observed behavior of brittle rocks under high strain-rate loading.
tldr: A crack-geometry-based model is proposed to describe permeability evolution in rocks under dynamic loading.
motivation: Accurate permeability representation is important for fluid extraction and containment in geological formations, but low-porosity brittle rocks are highly sensitive to pore geometry and connectivity, and dynamic permeability measurements are limited.
method: Rock void space is represented as an evolving network of penny-shaped cracks with prescribed orientations, where permeability changes are described via crack aperture, length, and spacing, including opening/closure, fracture-energy-driven propagation, plastic-strain-driven nucleation, coalescence, and strain-rate-dependent fracture toughening, implemented in the GeoDyn hydrocode.
result: The model shows a strong relation between permeability and crack length, with crack propagation playing a major role in permeability enhancement, while growth can be limited by poor connectivity and crack closure, capturing changes of several orders of magnitude depending on stress state, strain rate, crack orientation, and connectivity.
conclusion: The proposed crack-network model reproduces observed permeability behavior of brittle rocks under high strain-rate loading and provides a tool for assessing dynamic permeability evolution.

title: Inverse Optimal Feedback Stabilization Of 3d Nonholonomic Vehicles In Spherical Coordinates
authors: Kwang Hak Kim, Mamadou Diagne, Miroslav Krstic
abstract: ArXiv:2609.36212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inverse optimal control provides optimality and robustness guarantees without solving the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, but its application to 3D nonholonomic vehicles has been precluded by the absence of strict control Lyapunov functions (CLFs). Recently, such strict CLFs were constructed for the 3D nonholonomic vehicle in spherical coordinates, which circumvent Brockett's obstruction, on the largest possible domain. Building on this construction, this paper develops a general inverse optimal stabilizing controller for the 3D nonholonomic vehicle actuated by surge velocity, pitch rate, and yaw rate. The design is a damping [MATH] feedback that minimizes a meaningful cost and inherits stability margins. Its flexibility is demonstrated through two choices of penalty function: a quadratic running cost on the state, recovering a near-classical optimal control formulation, and stabilization under user-defined input constraints. Numerical simulations illustrate stabilization performance, control-effort tradeoffs, and the effect of input constraints.
tldr: Develops an inverse optimal stabilizing controller for a 3D nonholonomic vehicle in spherical coordinates using a recently constructed strict control Lyapunov function.
motivation: Inverse optimal control provides optimality and robustness without solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, but its application to 3D nonholonomic vehicles was previously blocked by the absence of strict control Lyapunov functions.
method: Building on a recent strict CLF construction, the paper designs a damping feedback controller that minimizes a meaningful cost, with two penalty function choices: quadratic state running cost and stabilization under user-defined input constraints.
result: Numerical simulations demonstrate stabilization performance, control-effort tradeoffs, and the effect of input constraints, showing the controller inherits stability margins.
conclusion: The proposed inverse optimal controller enables robust optimal stabilization of 3D nonholonomic vehicles in spherical coordinates, circumventing Brockett's obstruction.
